title: Big Four Firms Embrace AI to Revamp Corporate Service Offerings
author: Amanda Iacone

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts AI as a driver of work reallocation and operating-model redesign rather than wholesale human replacement, and materially extends the cluster by describing a managed-services model in which providers combine process transformation, shared technology and continuing professional work. Its claims of lower staffing and higher margins are projections with limited segment-level disclosure, and it does not address legal-specific verification or capability evidence.
qs: Transforming processes and layering on new technology in addition to the skills EY professionals provide are key components of the service, Hollingworth said.
They also bring a growing bench of experienced professionals to handle whatever the AI can’t.

kp.k: AI drives a pivot from advice to managed operations
kp.d: The article reports that Deloitte, EY, KPMG, and PwC are pursuing multi-year contracts to redesign and run corporate back-office functions as AI disrupts accounting and consulting. This is evidence about those industries, not a direct claim about legal services. The strategic exposure is substantial: consulting produces almost half of global revenue for EY, KPMG, and PwC and nearly two-thirds of Deloitte’s worldwide fees.
qs: The Big Four accounting and consulting firms are looking to stay competitive as artificial intelligence shakes up their industry by pivoting to focus on multi-year contracts meant to reinvent and run corporate back-office suites.
Consulting is elemental to the Big Four, producing almost half of global revenue for EY, KPMG, and PwC, and nearly two-thirds of Deloitte’s fees worldwide.

kp.k: Managed services combine operational responsibility, automation, and human expertise
kp.d: The reported model goes beyond outsourcing: firms take responsibility for critical functions, introduce new processes and technology, and retain experienced professionals for work AI cannot handle. Examples include anti-money laundering compliance and cybersecurity; EY’s Laurie Hollingworth identifies finance, risk, talent, and tax as core areas, serving clients from Fortune 500 companies to entities preparing to go public.
qs: Managed services offerings go beyond outsourcing, with firms taking ownership of critical tasks like anti-money laundering compliance for financial institutions or protecting data and IT infrastructure from cyber threats.
The firms install new processes for their clients, with fresh technology to automate and streamline the work.
They also bring a growing bench of experienced professionals to handle whatever the AI can’t.

kp.k: Reusable AI agents spread development costs across clients
kp.d: The article describes the firms’ pitch to corporate managers under pressure to adopt agentic AI: use portfolios of agents already built and tested by the Big Four rather than recreate capabilities internally. It argues that reuse improves efficiency for customers and providers by distributing technology development costs across multiple clients; it supplies no quantified efficiency results.
qs: For corporate managers under pressure to weave cutting edge [agentic AI](https://news.bloombergtax.com/financial-accounting/big-four-firms-roll-out-ai-that-can-handle-routine-tasks-solo) throughout the company, the pitch is simple: rely on a portfolio of AI agents the Big Four firms have already built and tested, with a library of new capabilities in the works, rather than recreating similar improvements on their own.
That’s more efficient for both customers and firms, which can spread out their technology development costs across multiple clients.

kp.k: Revenue targets indicate ambitions, not disclosed segment performance
kp.d: PwC’s Tim Canonico states a target of 20% to 25% of global advisory revenues, while KPMG targets 15% to 20% of US consulting fees. The article frames the broader growth ambitions as achievable within the next few years, not current revenue shares. Although all four firms highlight managed services in financial results, none discloses its segment revenue. EY declines to specify ambitions; Deloitte does not answer questions about size and growth, but reports growth in its “operate” business.
qs: The offering, known as managed services for corporate clients, could generate one-fifth of consulting revenue at some firms within the next few years, according to their own growth goals.

PwC has boosted hiring to meet increased demand as it aims for the offering to produce 20% to 25% of [global advisory revenues](https://news.bloombergtax.com/financial-accounting/pwc-reports-second-year-of-slower-revenue-growth-lags-peers), Canonico said.

KPMG has set a similar goal to grow its managed services to generate 15% to 20% of US consulting [fees](https://news.bloombergtax. /financial-accounting/kpmg-posts-5-global-growth-boosted-by-tax-managed-services).
None of them, however, detailed how much the segment generates.

kp.k: Demand growth prompts hiring despite labour-saving automation
kp.d: The article reports increased hiring at PwC and KPMG to meet managed-services demand, alongside its separate claim that agentic AI enables delivery with fewer people. KPMG’s Bassam Khattab identifies demand for AI-backed anti-money laundering tools and corporate finance applications. No headcount figures or net employment effect are provided.
qs: PwC has boosted hiring to meet increased demand as it aims for the offering to produce 20% to 25% of [global advisory revenues](https://news.bloombergtax.com/financial-accounting/pwc-reports-second-year-of-slower-revenue-growth-lags-peers), Canonico said.

The firm also is hiring to keep up with demand for AI-backed tools in areas like anti-money laundering for financial institutions and a suite of applications geared for corporate finance teams, said Bassam Khattab, US managed services leader for KPMG LLP.
The viability of agentic AI, however, has flipped that script, enabling firms to run corporate services with fewer people and higher margins.

kp.k: Agentic AI reportedly improves historically thin managed-services margins
kp.d: The article traces corporate tax department outsourcing deals to 2018 and describes traditional managed services as workforce-intensive and lower-margin than expensive advisory projects. It asserts that agentic AI changes those economics by reducing staffing requirements and raising margins. Accounting professor Hrish Desai endorses the economic-change argument, but the article provides no measured margin or productivity comparisons.
qs: Managed services itself isn’t new—firms began hoovering up corporate tax departments through outsourcing deals in [2018](https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report/in-house-tax-staff-you-may-get-invite-to-big-four-soon-1).
Historically those offerings required a large workforce and delivered thin profit margins, compared to high-priced advisory projects.
The viability of agentic AI, however, has flipped that script, enabling firms to run corporate services with fewer people and higher margins.
“AI changed the economics,” said Hrish Desai, associate accounting professor at Arkansas State University.

kp.k: Recurring contracts support cross-selling and revenue resilience
kp.d: The article argues that multi-year managed-services contracts can bundle advisory, tax, and assurance, generate recurring revenue, and expose client problems that create opportunities for additional advisory sales. It places the search for predictable income after a post-pandemic cycle of two years of soaring revenue followed by falling fees and layoffs. EY’s Hollingworth describes operational embeddedness as giving the firm access to strategic client conversations.
qs: Managed services contracts spanning multiple years often bundle together offerings that can cut across advisory, tax, and assurance—amplifying the financial impact for the Big Four.
Multi-year deals, with recurring revenue, enable firms to spot pain points and emerging risks—opportunities to cross-sell additional services, including more lucrative advisory work.

Firms are seeking more predictable sources of income after the post-pandemic boom and bust business cycle that featured two years of soaring revenues followed by a sudden drop off in fees and a wave of [layoffs](https://news.bloombergtax.com/financial-accounting/big-four-reshape-consulting-workforce-strategy-with-rare-layoffs).
“It puts us in very strategic conversations with our clients,” she said. “You become part of the fabric of their operation.”

kp.k: Technology competitors threaten incumbent positioning and reshape pricing
kp.d: The article reports that broader service offerings require new pricing structures, without specifying particular fee models. It also identifies competition from technology giants and AI vendors and notes OpenAI and Palantir partnerships with Accenture, Cognizant, and other consultancies. K2 Consulting Research’s Tom Rodenhauser presents eventual erosion of the Big Four’s market position as a risk, not an established outcome.
qs: Firms are navigating a shifting landscape as a broader menu of services demands new [pricing](https://news.bloombergtax.com/financial-accounting/ai-efficiency-gains-push-accounting-firms-to-reimagine-pricing) structures for how they charge clients.
The Big Four also face increasing competition from tech giants, along with other AI vendors, to develop in-demand AI tools and agents for clients.
Tech-native players like OpenAI and Palantir Technologies Inc. have inked partnerships with Accenture, Cognizant, and other consulting firms to help corporate clients adopt AI.
The risk is that those technology firms eventually could undermine the Big Four’s premier position in the market, Rodenhauser said.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is driving the Big Four toward multi-year managed services that transform and operate corporate functions rather than merely provide advice.
pts.d: In this cross-domain article, Amanda Iacone describes changes in accounting, consulting and corporate back-office services, not specifically legal services. She reports that client demand for AI-enabled workflows is expanding managed services across advisory, tax and assurance. Firms implement technology and processes, take responsibility for operational tasks, and supply experienced professionals for work AI cannot handle. PwC's Tim Canonico identifies managed services as a major strategic growth driver; EY's Laurie Hollingworth describes the resulting deeper integration with clients' operations.

pts.k: Reusable AI capabilities and reduced staffing requirements are said to improve managed-services economics.
pts.d: Iacone reports that using the Big Four's existing portfolios of AI agents instead of building equivalent capabilities internally can be more efficient for corporate clients and allows providers to spread development costs across clients. She also asserts that viable agentic AI enables delivery with fewer people and higher margins, reversing the historically labour-intensive, thin-margin economics of managed services. These are reported mechanisms, not quantified productivity or margin findings. Accounting professor Hrish Desai supports the economic-change interpretation.

pts.k: Managed services are positioned as a growing, more resilient revenue source with opportunities to sell additional advisory work.
pts.d: Iacone reports company ambitions rather than achieved revenue shares: Canonico says PwC aims for managed services to produce 20%–25% of global advisory revenue, while KPMG targets 15%–20% of US consulting fees. She argues that recurring multi-year contracts improve income predictability and reveal client needs that can generate additional, more lucrative advisory work.

pts.k: AI changes competitive dynamics and may threaten the Big Four's market position.
pts.d: Iacone describes competition from technology companies and AI vendors to supply corporate AI tools and agents, alongside pressure to change pricing structures as service offerings broaden. K2 Consulting Research's Tom Rodenhauser characterises the Big Four's core business as disrupted and warns that technology firms could eventually undermine their leading market position. KPMG's Bassam Khattab expresses a broader prediction that AI has the potential to revolutionise consulting.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article relies on executive interviews, company financial reporting, service examples and expert interpretation, rather than measured AI performance or disclosed segment economics.
pts.d: Company executives supply growth goals, hiring reports and descriptions of client demand. Examples include KPMG's anti-money-laundering and corporate-finance tools, EY's operation of finance, risk, talent and tax functions, and Deloitte's electronic health records service. Iacone cites partnerships involving OpenAI, Palantir and consulting firms as context for competitive change. Rodenhauser and Desai provide expert interpretations. No Big Four firm discloses managed-services revenue in the article; EY does not disclose revenue ambitions, and Deloitte does not answer questions about size and growth. No quantified staffing reductions, margin improvements, client savings or AI benchmarks are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes a current transition in 2026, near-term growth ambitions and an undated longer-term competitive risk.
pts.d: Demand growth, hiring and service transformation are presented as underway at publication. The article places the broad revenue-share ambition within the next few years, without specifying separate deadlines for PwC and KPMG. Contracts run for multiple years. Efficiency claims depend on reusable AI capabilities and the viability of agentic AI, with professionals retained to handle tasks beyond AI's capabilities. Rodenhauser's competitive warning is explicitly a possibility that could materialise eventually, not an established outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are Big Four providers, corporate clients, service-delivery professionals and competing technology businesses.
pts.d: The Big Four seek growth, better margins, recurring income and closer client relationships. Corporate managers and functions such as finance, risk, talent, tax, compliance and IT receive transformed and externally operated workflows. Clients include financial institutions, Fortune 500 companies and businesses preparing to go public. Professionals continue to handle work AI cannot perform; the article reports hiring at PwC and KPMG alongside the claim that AI reduces staffing required for delivery, without quantifying net employment effects. Technology firms are both partners in adoption and potential competitors. The article does not establish effects on law firms, lawyers or access to justice.
